doc.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Teaching himself guitar; Django, George Barnes, Chicken a la Swing
summary: He learns guitar from records, then Django and George Barnes parts and the Pizzarelli rite-of-passage duet.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Yeah. And so there were the chords, now see? And it works with the records. So I’d play along with records. And gravitated toward learning Peter Frampton solos and all that, that went along with that. I mean my father had amps and guitars, so I was the guy. “Come on over, we’ve got the equipment.” Plugging everything into one amplifier, the whole band came out. And so along the way my father said, “Well okay” actually he tells it, which is strange, is that there was a trombone player a couple of towns over who wanted to play “Spain” like at a talent show at his high school. So we had this record and so I was like okay, so I had to go [scats], that was the fastest thing I’d ever played in my life [scats]. So it was a big deal. So I learned this thing and my father was like amazed I guess. And I can imagine, that out of the clear blue sky we’re playing “Spain.” And so he went okay — here’s a Django Reinhardt record. Listen to “Rose Room.” And here’s this guy going [scats]. Jeez. Okay. Well I’ll try some of that. And then we started in with the George Barnes-Bucky Pizzarelli records. And he’d say, “Why don’t you listen to George?” And I’d start to learn George’s parts, and we’d play them around the house. And so the jazz vocabulary was making its way into my head. And I would go, whenever he’d play a concert somewhere I’d go and play “Honeysuckle Rose” at the end of the concert with him, because I knew George’s part and I could play his solo pretty poorly, so, hence, that was my thing. And then he taught me “Chicken a la Swing” that Carl Kress/Dick © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
McDonough duet and I played the second part. That was sort of a rite of passage for the Pizzarellis. Because Mary had learned it previously when she was fifteen. A very hip family.

I went to Florida once and I was jamming with Jack Petersen, a great guitar player down there. And he’d say, “What do you want to play?” And I said, “I want to play “Chicken a la Swing,” and he knew the first part. And I said how many guys are jamming “Chicken a la Swing?” Everybody else would call like “Monk’s Mood.” No we were playing “Chicken a la Swing.” So there was all this guitar stuff going on, and that’s how the guitar all started.
I mean I was hearing Ray Conniff when I grew up. Wow.
